focus_profile.theme: 周三：财险、车险与巨灾风险
focus_profile.learning_goal: 关注车险定价、巨灾风险、责任险、费用率、赔付率和外部生态数据。
tasks: 选择一条财险或车险新闻，找出影响赔付频率或案均赔款的变量。
写出一个巨灾或新能源车险的风险分层思路。
记录一个可用于定价或反欺诈的数据源。

daily_concept.definition: 赔款及相关理赔成本相对保费的比例，是健康险、财险和车险经验分析核心指标。
daily_concept.exercise: 把赔付率拆成出险频率、案均赔款、责任结构和渠道质量四个驱动。

items.original_title: Independent Agents - A Forward View
items.rss_title: Independent Agents - A Forward View
items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.original_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_description: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:06 Insurers aren't avoiding AI due to fear—they're waiting for core platform vendors to deliver native capabilities instead of risky integrations. October 22, 2026 Image We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI; they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase; it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. What This Means If You're Evaluating Tools Right Now A few things are worth doing before you sign anything: Separating "edge" AI from "core" AI. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. Testing whether the value is domain-specific. James Ballot Diane Brassard October 22, 2026 We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. If a vendor's edge could be replicated by connecting a general-purpose model (for example, an enterprise assistant such as Microsoft Copilot, or an AI workflow that retrieves and summarizes documents) to your own policy forms, endorsements, claim files, and underwriting guidelines, don't count on that edge lasting once your core system catches up. items.rss_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_description: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/26/2026 - 17:11 Bill Gross recently announced a free database of AI-generated ideas for innovative companies, based on the 31 methodologies that he's developed over the past three decades and that have powered his Idealab incubator. The list of ideas — currently totaling a whopping 1,208,580 — may or may not contain an idea that you'll be able to turn into big bucks, but I think that exploring the database and interacting with the ideas is worth a bit of your time. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. items.title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.original_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_description: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

items.title: Meta and Snap Face Major Legal Test of Youth Social Media Addiction Claims
items.original_title: Meta and Snap Face Major Legal Test of Youth Social Media Addiction Claims
items.rss_title: Meta and Snap Face Major Legal Test of Youth Social Media Addiction Claims
items.rss_description: Two teenage plaintiffs who say social media caused them to develop serious mental health problems will take Meta Platforms and Snap to trial in Los Angeles on Oct. 28 in the latest test of claims raised in thousands of US …
items.extracted_text: Meta and Snap Face Major Legal Test of Youth Social Media Addiction Claims Article 0 Comments Two teenage plaintiffs who say social media caused them to develop serious mental health problems will take Meta Platforms and Snap to trial in Los Angeles on Oct. 28 in the latest test of claims raised in thousands of US lawsuits over social media’s impact on young people. The case is only the second to go to trial involving individual plaintiffs who allege that social media companies deliberately designed their platforms to be addictive. Social media companies lost the first such trial to the tune of $6 million in damages in March. Plaintiffs referred to in court papers as S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old woman from Mississippi, have said they began using YouTube as early as age 3 or 4 and other platforms around age 9. They have alleged that autoplay, infinite scroll and other features drove them to compulsive use, and they developed depression, anxiety and eating disorders as a result. Related Stories: Meta Agrees to Pay Up to $18 Billion Over Social Media Claims Appeals Court: Social Media Companies Must Face Thousands of Addiction Lawsuits FTC Probing YouTube Over Social Media Policies TikTok Reaches First State Settlement Over Teen Safety Claims, Agrees to User Limits The trial, which begins with the jury selection process on Wednesday, is expected to run for several weeks. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram head Adam Mosseri and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel are expected to testify. The two plaintiffs initially sued TikTok and Alphabet’s YouTube, in addition to Meta and Snap. Both reached settlements with TikTok and YouTube ahead of trial, and the Illinois plaintiff also settled with Meta. Wednesday’s trial covers claims by both plaintiffs against Snap, and the Mississippi plaintiff’s claims against Meta. Meta and Snap have asked Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn Kuhl, presiding over the proceedings, to split the cases into separate trials, arguing that trying them together would unfairly mix up the evidence for jurors. The judge has not yet ruled on that request. ‘A Young Person’s Mental Health’ A Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with the claims made against it and has built protections into its platforms for a decade. Meta owns Instagram and Facebook. “A young person’s mental health is shaped by many factors, as the evidence in this trial will show,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The plaintiff used TikTok far more than Instagram or Facebook, and her personal circumstances were a substantial factor in her struggles.” A Snap spokesperson said its Snapchat platform is different from traditional social media because it does not open to a feed or a ranking of what other people post. The company has built safeguards into its platform, the spokesperson said. “We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent their experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed,” the spokesperson said. Emily Jeffcott, an attorney representing the Mississippi plaintiff, said in a statement ahead of the trial that “we look forward to educating the jury about the dangers of features like endless feeds, autoplay and streaks and how Meta – and allegedly Snap as well – have implemented and emphasized these features.” A Test Case Plaintiffs S.J. and K.D.B. sued in 2023. Both described staying awake for hours scrolling social media, losing focus in class and engaging in self-harm using methods shown in social media videos. They are seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages. Their cases are among more than 3,000 lawsuits brought by individuals and others that have been consolidated in Los Angeles Superior Court. Their lawsuits have been selected as bellwethers, or test cases, meaning the verdict could influence how the companies and plaintiffs resolve the remaining cases. Social media companies have denied that their platforms were designed to addict young people, and have said they have taken action to make the apps safe for young users. They also have argued that they are shielded from the claims by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 1996 federal law that generally protects online platforms from liability over user-generated content. The trial judge disagreed that Section 230 bars claims over how the sites are designed, and allowed the suits by the two plaintiffs to go to trial. In the case decided in March, a Los Angeles jury found that Meta and YouTube were negligent, siding with a young woman referred to in court papers as Kaley G.M. There have been multiple cases scheduled for trial since then, but the companies have settled the claims or, in some cases, the plaintiffs have chosen to drop them. School District and States Sue More than 3,800 lawsuits brought by states, school districts and individuals over similar claims are pending in federal court in California, court records showed. In August, Meta reached settlements worth up to $18 billion to resolve claims made by nearly every US state and territory over the impact of its platforms on teen mental health. The company agreed as part of that deal to change how teens can access Instagram and Facebook. Members of Meta’s senior legal team told reporters after that settlement that the company views the individual and school district cases as harder to prove at trial than cases brought by states because they require plaintiffs to directly link specific problems to its social media platforms. Meta is appealing the verdict in the case decided in March, arguing that Section 230 should have barred the claims by plaintiff Kaley G.M. A ruling in Meta’s favor on the issue could derail thousands of lawsuits over youth mental health and shield it from billions of dollars in potential liability that the company has said poses a serious threat to its future, according to experts. items.extracted_text: AI Cybersecurity Startup Upwind Raises at $3.8 Billion Value Article 0 Comments Upwind Security, a San Francisco-based startup offering cybersecurity for artificial intelligence and cloud applications, has secured $400 million in fresh financing that values the company at $3.8 billion. Bessemer Venture Partners led the investment, with participation from existing backers including Greylock Partners and Craft Ventures, Upwind told Bloomberg News. Some details of the round were previously reported by Bloomberg News. The startup has raised $830 million since its founding in 2022 and was last valued at $1.5 billion in January. Upwind’s platform detects threats in companies’ cloud infrastructure, such as malware or suspicious activity, and gives them visibility into those vulnerabilities. Earlier this year, the startup expanded the platform to mitigate risks from AI. Cybersecurity is evolving as AI models becoming more adept at finding and potentially exploiting software weaknesses at unprecedented speed and scale. Last week, governments and companies around the world pulled down their sites as a protective measure after security researchers, assisted by AI, discovered two flaws in PHP, a programming language that underpins much of the internet. The growing threat has led to a flurry of venture capital investments in security companies seeking to plug such weaknesses. “In the last three months, there was more activity than in the last four years combined,” said Chief Executive Officer Amiram Shachar in an interview, pointing to proliferating attacks, breaches and zero-day flaws, industry terminology for previously undisclosed security weaknesses. “The cost or the knowledge for people to start hacking or doing reconnaissance or doing manipulations or behaving maliciously is down to zero when you have an AI tool,” he added. The startup is approaching $100 million in annual recurring revenue, a projection of annual revenue based on a shorter time period, by the end of the year, he said. Upwind plans to use the investment for engineering development and to bolster its sales and marketing efforts, according to Shachar. The startup employs some 600 workers in the US, Israel, Europe and Asia. Photo: Photographer: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.extracted_text: GEICO Returns $10.5 Million to New Jersey Policyholders Article 0 Comments The New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance has ordered GEICO to return more than $10.5 million in wrongfully-charged premium back to policyholders. The department also issued a penalty of $1.2 million to GEICO and its affiliates for improper business practices. The returned premiums and penalty are the result of a market conduct exam that covered GEICO’s private passenger automobile insurance business during the period June 1, 2023 to May 31, 2024 in response to consumer complaints. During the course of the examination, the department identified what it called a “systemic pattern of improper practices” affecting more than 15,000 policyholders across multiple GEICO companies. The department’s examination cited the company in four areas: charging rates higher than what were previously approved by the department cancelling policies for improper reasons failing to disclose required language on notices that could lead to policy nonrenewal and failing to make total loss vehicle owners who retain the vehicle after settlement aware of their rights. The department said GEICO voluntarily began issuing refunds during the examination process as the errors were identified. Topics New Jersey Was this article valuable? items.original_title: Trading Platform Rocked by Japan Hack, $50 Million Ransom
items.rss_title: Trading Platform Rocked by Japan Hack, $50 Million Ransom
items.rss_description: Hackers targeting a currency trading platform claimed to have published customer information after failing to receive a $50 million ransom, adding to a wave of cyberattacks in Japan that have prompted the government to draw up emergency measures. GMO Internet …
items.extracted_text: Trading Platform Rocked by Japan Hack, $50 Million Ransom Article 0 Comments Hackers targeting a currency trading platform claimed to have published customer information after failing to receive a $50 million ransom, adding to a wave of cyberattacks in Japan that have prompted the government to draw up emergency measures. GMO Internet Group Inc., the subject of the latest attack, asked customers to scan their PCs for viruses, back up their files and unplug and turn off their devices, saying it would not agree to the hackers’ demands. The company hasn’t confirmed a follow-up ransomware attack, which the hackers had also threatened. Some clients had earlier flagged transactions they hadn’t initiated. Related: Japan Takaichi Orders Cybersecurity Measures as Attacks Grow A GMO spokesperson said its trading service had been suspended since Oct. 21, with the company also pausing new subscriptions. Every user of Onamae.com could be affected after all the cloud service’s servers were compromised, they added. On Monday, GMO’s shares tumbled the most since 2011 as concerns over the impact of a cyberattack deepened. GMO asked the government over the weekend to deploy active cyber defense after its services were subjected to unauthorized access. With dozens of businesses in Japan reporting breaches to their systems and potential leaks of client data in recent weeks, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said the nation would address the damage from the latest attack with a sense of urgency. Katayama said there was “a sense of crisis shared globally” over cybersecurity as hackers harness artificial intelligence to take advantage of vulnerabilities. “Given how rapidly these incidents and circumstances evolve, we will continue to call on financial authorities to respond appropriately and swiftly as developments unfold,” she told reporters. The finance minister said earlier that five foreign exchange firms had reported customers affected by the GMO incident. She added that she had received no reports of new unauthorized transactions. GMO sought government assistance on Saturday to help disrupt the source of the attacks. Hackers claim to have published personal information on one GMO customer, NHK reported without attribution. Emergency Measures Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi instructed her cabinet on Monday to draw up emergency measures by the end of next week in response to the spate of cyberattacks. Marito Ueda, president of SBI FX Trade, said the retail currency trading industry as a whole has recently been seeing customers closing dormant accounts, and that with interest rates rising, he expected some people to opt to put money back into bank deposits. “Yet, those who were actively trading FX appear to have stayed in the market, as trading volumes have not declined,” he said. “If the fallout extends beyond FX and into equities for instance, it could become much harder to contain.” At a regular press conference on Tuesday, economy minister Ryosei Akazawa said the government would offer smaller companies free consultation services on boosting their cybersecurity. Cyberattacks and the discovery of vulnerabilities in PHP programming language used in some websites have made a swift response an urgent priority for businesses and the government. Several political parties called for stronger measures last week. In recommendations submitted to Takaichi last week, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party said the recent wave of cyberattacks constituted a serious crisis that could be described as “the eve of a cyber emergency,” threatening Japan’s national security. It warned that “AI cyber saturation attacks,” in which the technology automatically identifies system vulnerabilities and launches attacks simultaneously, could occur in the near future. The party also proposed creating a response headquarters led by the prime minister’s office, while accelerating efforts to improve the capabilities of the Self-Defense Forces and police and strengthen cooperation with allies. In the financial sector, it called for the public and private sectors to work together to steadily implement defensive measures. ‘AI Versus Humans’ Masaaki Taira, a former digital minister who led the drafting of the recommendations, said attackers are using AI to mount hacks faster and on a broader scale than before, while companies are still relying on people to defend themselves. “Structurally, it has become AI versus humans,” he said. The government needs to work with leading AI companies to build a system capable of using AI for defense, he added. “The recent surge in AI-enabled breaches of Japanese web-based systems has already led to the thefts of 187 million people’s personal information in total,” said Mihoko Matsubara, chief cybersecurity strategist at NTT Inc. “Global cyber defenders including Japan are struggling to keep up with the speed and scale of AI-enabled cyberattacks.” One common concern is securing specialist personnel. With highly skilled private-sector cybersecurity professionals such as white-hat hackers in mind, the LDP called for the creation of a new personnel and compensation system that would “break through the rigidities of the civil-service system and enable compensation commensurate with market value.” Behind these proposals is a recognition that government salaries are insufficient compared with those in the private sector. According to the National Personnel Authority, the government can offer annual compensation of as much as ¥33.8 million ($214,000) under its fixed-term appointment system to private-sector personnel with specialized expertise. items.title: Safety gaps leave new employees vulnerable beyond orientation
items.original_title: Safety gaps leave new employees vulnerable beyond orientation
items.rss_title: Safety gaps leave new employees vulnerable beyond orientation
items.rss_description: Safety professionals say employers seeking to reduce injuries among first-year workers should look beyond orientation to how supervisors verify skills, how mentors demonstrate safe practices and how employees raise concerns.
items.extracted_text: Assumptions about prior experience and understanding of training can leave new hires exposed, especially when turnover and pressure to fill positions strain employers’ resources. A September Workers Compensation Research Institute report found employees in their first year accounted for 39% of injuries in 2022-2024, while those with less than two years’ tenure accounted for 54%. Separately, Travelers’ latest injury impact report released in May found first-year employees accounted for roughly 37% of injuries and 34% of claim costs, according to its analysis of over 1.2 million workers compensation claims from 2021 through 2025. “I think they’re missing the mark because they’re making these assumptions,” said Katherine Mendoza, Fox Lake, Illinois-based senior director of workplace safety programs at the National Safety Council. Employers sometimes give experienced hires insufficient attention because they have worked in the same industry, said Chris Hayes, Hartford, Connecticut-based assistant vice president of risk control at Travelers. “And the reality is that even if you’re moving within the same industry, you’re still a new employee and you’re still at risk,” he added. Differences in operating pace, management and workplace practices require adjustment, Mr. Hayes said. Employers should identify hazardous tasks and establish safe methods with input from management, frontline employees and union representatives where applicable. Choosing who teaches those methods also matters. Assigning a longtime employee to train a newcomer can perpetuate shortcuts if the mentor’s practices conflict with established procedures, he said. Employers often treat orientation as a single event and assume attendance translates into understanding, Ms. Mendoza said. A separate safety orientation can give the subject needed attention, but safe onboarding should continue through scheduled checkpoints, such as at 30, 60 and 90 days, she said. Supervisors and mentors should observe employees performing tasks and determine whether they can work safely independently. Readiness should reflect demonstrated competency, Ms. Mendoza said, because employees learn at different speeds and some tasks take longer to master. Repeated hiring can make it difficult for employers to revisit training and confirm that workers understand changing exposures, said Ahren Hohenwarter, head of risk management at ICW Group, based in Pleasanton, California. “Without confirmation of understanding, the training really is just a check mark in an onboarding packet,” he said. Training must accommodate differences in language and literacy, using demonstrations and hands-on instruction alongside other methods, he said. Employers also need to assign capable people to oversee the process and provide sufficient time and funding. ICW’s published first-year injury prevention guidance recommends practical assessments before independent work, follow-up safety check-ins and refresher training as duties change. It also advises employers to observe actual work practices and address fatigue and workload early in employment. High turnover strengthens the case for that investment, Mr. Hayes said. Injuries disrupt operations, require coworkers to cover absences and can contribute to employees leaving. Workers also need confidence that asking questions will be welcomed. Ms. Mendoza said new hires may hesitate to admit confusion while trying to prove they can perform efficiently. Employers should make speaking up an expectation from the outset, with clear channels for reporting hazards and alternatives when employees are uncomfortable approaching supervisors, said Mr. Hohenwarter. Such reports give employers a chance to correct conditions before someone is hurt, Mr. Hayes said. Building trust can help bring persistent hazards, such as a kitchen floor that repeatedly gets wet, to management’s attention, he said. items.title: Court rejects Delta workers comp benefit reduction
items.original_title: Court rejects Delta workers comp benefit reduction
items.rss_title: Court rejects Delta workers comp benefit reduction
items.rss_description: A Georgia appeals court on Monday ruled that Delta Air Lines improperly reduced an injured employee’s workers compensation benefits based on a medical report that did not establish he could return to work.
items.extracted_text: Jorge Lamar injured his lumbar spine while lifting baggage for Delta and began receiving temporary total disability benefits of $725 a week in September 2022. He challenged the airline’s subsequent reduction of those payments, according to Jorge F. Lamar v. Delta Airlines , Inc. et al., decided by the Court of Appeals of Georgia. Delta filed a notice in August 2023 stating that Mr. Lamar’s authorized treating physician had released him to work with restrictions. The airline attached a July 17, 2023, medical report from the physician, Dr. Donald Langenbeck. The report instructed Mr. Lamar not to lift more than 15 pounds, prescribed medication and directed him to attend work-conditioning physical therapy before a follow-up appointment. It did not specifically release him to return to work. Delta converted his benefits to temporary partial disability payments of $438 a week effective July 2024. An administrative law judge upheld the reduction, concluding that the lifting restriction established Mr. Lamar could return to work. The Appellate Division of the State Board of Workers’ Compensation adopted that ruling, and the Superior Court of Fulton County affirmed. The appeals court reversed, finding that the medical report did not demonstrate Mr. Lamar could work with restrictions. It said the 15-pound limit repeated an existing restriction and, by itself, did not establish a release to light-duty work under the circumstances. The court also rejected reliance on older medical reports outside the applicable 60-day window. It directed that the case return to the workers compensation board for an award consistent with its opinion and consideration of whether attorney fees should be awarded. items.title: Edison Must Face Jury Over Equipment’s Role in Massive California Fire
items.original_title: Edison Must Face Jury Over Equipment’s Role in Massive California Fire
items.rss_title: Edison Must Face Jury Over Equipment’s Role in Massive California Fire
items.rss_description: A judge ruled that Southern California Edison cannot escape a trial over a central claim in lawsuits over 2025’s Eaton Fire, the most destructive blaze in the Los Angeles area’s history. Superior Court Judge Laura Seigle rejected a request by …
items.extracted_text: Edison Must Face Jury Over Equipment’s Role in Massive California Fire Article 0 Comments A judge ruled that Southern California Edison cannot escape a trial over a central claim in lawsuits over 2025’s Eaton Fire, the most destructive blaze in the Los Angeles area’s history. Superior Court Judge Laura Seigle rejected a request by the Edison International unit to rule that property owners who suffered billions of dollars in losses in the January 2025 fire near Pasadena have no recourse under a California law that holds utilities automatically liable when their equipment starts a blaze. Related: Edison Drops on Willful Misconduct Allegations in Eaton Fire Case Seigle’s ruling means that Edison and fire victims’ lawyers will spar at an initial trial set for late January over so-called inverse condemnation, a state legal doctrine that can put utilities on the hook for all property damages from fires even if the company didn’t act negligently. Attorneys for the insurance companies that have paid out damage claims previously tried to get the issue decided in their favor without a trial to recoup their payouts from Edison, but Seigle rejected their request. David Eisenhauer, a spokesperson for SCE, said the utility disagrees with the court’s latest ruling. “We will continue through the court process and encourage those directly impacted by the Eaton Fire to file claims through the Wildfire Recovery Compensation Program rather than pursuing lengthy and uncertain litigation,” Eisenhauer said in a statement. Related: Southern California Edison Chief Warns Wildfire Impasse Risks Higher Customer Bills A report by the Los Angeles County Fire Department in early August concluded the Eaton Fire was caused by electrical arcing events that took place on an out-of-service tower on a dry hillside. The fire killed 19 people, destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses and burned 14,000 acres. Edison Chief Executive Officer Pedro Pizarro told investors in late July that “no other viable alternatives have appeared” aside from the company’s equipment that would explain how the wildfire erupted. Lawyers suing Edison allege that a Jan. 7 power surge on a nearby, active line created a magnetic field that briefly reenergized the dormant cable, setting off the sparks that ignited the blaze. SCE has argued in court filings that the transmission tower where the Eaton Fire allegedly ignited had been idle for so long, since 1971, that it no longer qualifies as the kind of public infrastructure that triggers California’s strict liability rule for utilities. In her latest ruling, Seigle cast doubt on Edison’s attempts to shore up its arguments by citing past court cases. Edison “did not cite any legal authority that a transmission line originally built to serve the public cannot be a public improvement because it was idle and not transmitting electricity at the time of the harm,” she wrote. items.title: US Tells Ships to Avoid Unnecessary Transits Through Hormuz
items.original_title: US Tells Ships to Avoid Unnecessary Transits Through Hormuz
items.rss_title: US Tells Ships to Avoid Unnecessary Transits Through Hormuz
items.rss_description: The US military said vessels that have no need to move between ports in the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz should stay away, as tensions ratchet up in the region. “Due to the current geopolitical situation, vessels …
items.extracted_text: US Tells Ships to Avoid Unnecessary Transits Through Hormuz Article 0 Comments The US military said vessels that have no need to move between ports in the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz should stay away, as tensions ratchet up in the region. “Due to the current geopolitical situation, vessels which do not need to transit the area are advised to remain well clear to avoid unnecessary delays to their voyage,” the US Naval Forces Central Command said in an advisory on Wednesday issued via the Joint Maritime Information Center. “Vessels transiting this area are advised to plan additional transit time to allow for increased traffic density and military blockade enforcement operations,” the notice said. It remains unclear what prompted the advisory. The US military last publicly issued a similar notice in mid-July, when it began its blockade of Iranian shipping. Back then, it said that the blockade would not impede neutral passage through Hormuz, though ships should expect to be questioned on their intentions. Traffic through the chokepoint has recovered in recent months, with shuttle tankers making up a big part of the traffic carrying crude oil. These ships make multiple runs in and out of the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, where other tankers unwilling to risk the Strait await to receive cargoes. Dozens of crude tankers willing to take the risk have helped lift oil flows from the Persian Gulf to near prewar levels, while the US blockade has pushed Iranian crude exports close to zero. At the same time, Iran has been ramping up its attacks on ships to a wartime high of almost 30 in October. The latest US advisory said that neutral vessels with neutral cargo or are in ballast sailing between these neutral ports may be subject to questioning, visit, and search to confirm their intentions regarding the blockade. The US Central Command and the US Naval Forces Central Command — the naval unit that is part of Centcom and oversees the naval blockade of Iran — did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.
